prize_parts.citation: for empirical analysis of how technological change, the task content of work and import competition reshape labour demand, the wage structure and the adjustment of local labour markets

statement.case_for: My laureate set for B038 is unchanged. I changed the citation wording and one alternative. The reason is that the round-1 exchange sharpened what I think the achievement is. It is the evidence that technology and trade act on labour demand through measurable, distinct channels, and it covers who gains, who loses and how local labour markets adjust. The long-run wage-structure benchmark (Katz, on the race between education and technology) and the local-labour-market designs for trade exposure (Autor, Hanson, with Dorn on the China-shock papers) answer one question with a shared empirical toolkit. They are not merely two literatures joined by a shared author. I keep Katz in the third slot because the technology and wage-structure strand is the older and more foundational half of the evidence base. Without it the prize becomes a trade-shock prize, with the more contested magnitudes carrying the whole citation. I now word the citation around the empirical contribution and not the whole task framework. This is deliberate, to avoid claiming the conceptual priority of Acemoglu, Levy and Murnane. It also states which of Katz's contributions is recognised (wage structure and education versus technology), as Strömberg asked. Maturity is ample: the core work runs from the early 1990s into the 2010s, and the designs have been replicated, challenged and extended. The magnitude and persistence of the China-shock effects are still debated, but that bears on how the citation is phrased and not on whether the effects exist. I rest the case on these points and not on how many colleagues ranked it highly.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is unchanged and I cannot remove it. The three-name cap excludes Dorn, a full co-author of the central China-shock papers, and the task framework has contributors outside the ballot. The one-versus-two-discoveries question is a judgement, and several colleagues who respect the work (Krusell, Hjalmarsson, Enflo, Teorell) judge the credit boundary here to be less clean than for B044. Shift-share identification and the persistence of the effects remain contested. The adjacent 2021, 2023 and 2024 prizes may reduce the marginal case. I count that as a timing consideration only where an earlier citation covered the same discovery, and I do not think the written citations did. It is also a risk to the prize that five members currently prefer B044 and four prefer B038. No ballot has six votes, and a prize that cannot assemble a majority has a practical weakness regardless of scientific merit.

responses.point: Krusell moved his preferred part from B017 to B044 and keeps B038 as an alternative. He is less sure it is one discovery, since it joins a skill-premium literature with a trade-shock literature and the task framework has contributors outside the list. He judges B044 easier to cite cleanly.
responses.response: I accept that B044 has the more singular originating paper, and I count that as a real advantage for a short citation. I do not think the B038 split is as large as you suggest. The wage-structure benchmark and the trade-shock designs are read against each other in the same papers, and Autor is the common thread. I also note that B044 has its own boundary problem (Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum), so neither ballot has a clean credit line. If the committee rules that these are two discoveries, I agree with you that the trade-shock part should then be credited to Autor, Dorn and Hanson, with Dorn displacing Katz. I would not keep the trio and call it one achievement merely because it is convenient. I read it as one question at the level of labour demand, and I hold that view with uncertainty.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B044 first and B038 an alternative. She gives B038 less weight on maturity because shift-share identification and China-shock persistence are still debated, and she says she would support B038 if the committee finds a convincing way to credit Dorn.
responses.response: On maturity, I think the debate concerns the size and persistence of the effects and not whether import exposure shifts local labour demand. The Katz and Autor wage-structure and task evidence has been tested for far longer than the trade-shock papers. I agree that the Dorn problem is the real cost, and I do not have a way around it inside the cap. Adding Dorn means dropping Hanson or Katz. Dropping Hanson loses the multi-country regional-adjustment evidence. Dropping Katz narrows the prize to trade. I would rather state that cost openly than hide it. Your earlier acknowledgement that B044 is more theoretical than quasi-experimental work is a candid point about familiarity. I try to guard against the same bias, because B038 is close to the questions I work on.

responses.point: Hassler, as chair, prefers B037 and proposed only Autor and Hanson for B038 in his opening. He says the ballot combines two separable strands, that any three-name boundary omits a claimant, and that he would revisit it if the committee agreed a principled boundary.
responses.response: I propose a principle: each credited name anchors an identified, documented strand of the same labour-demand question. Katz anchors the long-run wage-structure benchmark, Autor the task and trade-shock designs, and Hanson the regional-adjustment evidence. The cost is Dorn, and I state it. An Autor and Hanson award would be principled only if the citation were deliberately narrowed to trade and local labour markets, and I would accept that version as a fallback on those terms. On the 2023 overlap with Goldin, I read that prize as recognising women's labour-market outcomes, so Katz's wage-structure evidence was not covered. I have not checked the 2023 background, so I treat this as adjacency and not duplication. On B037, I still lack an answer to how much of the collateral-amplification case is distinct from the 2022 recognition, and I am not persuaded that clean attribution settles it.

responses.point: Enflo ranks B044 first and B038 second. She argues that B038's credit boundary is blurred by neighbouring prizes and by two distinct strands, that Acemoglu's recognition in 2024 overlaps the task framework, and that the committee should say which strand carries the discovery.
responses.response: I take the request to say which strand carries the discovery. My answer is that the discovery is the empirical demonstration that technology and trade act on labour demand through measurable channels, which is neither strand alone. The citation should say that, and should not claim the conceptual task framework, which is where the Acemoglu, Levy and Murnane priority sits. The 2024 prize addressed institutions and prosperity. I do not see the empirical labour-demand evidence in that citation, though I have not verified the 2024 background in detail. I also concede your central point. B044 has a more singular origin. If the committee finds that B038 cannot be cited cleanly, I regard B044 as the strongest alternative on scientific grounds and not only on the numbers.

uncertainties: Whether the committee treats the wage-structure and technology strand and the China-shock strand as one achievement or two. This determines whether Katz or Dorn holds the third slot, and I cannot settle it from the supplied evidence.

How large and persistent the China-shock effects are, and how sensitive they are to shift-share identification and period. I am relying on the openings and my own knowledge, not on a fresh reanalysis.
How much of the empirical labour-demand evidence the 2021, 2023 and 2024 citations already covered. I have not checked those scientific backgrounds.

Whether B038 can reach six votes. If it cannot, my fallback is B044 (Melitz, Helpman), accepted on merit grounds: a single originating model, over twenty years of confirmation, and a distinct advance on the 2008 recognition. The cost is the uncredited empirical originators (Bernard, Jensen, Eaton, Kortum). I do not regard this as a case for artificial consensus.
For B037, the distinctness of the collateral-amplification channel from the 2022 prize and the thinness of direct empirical evidence. I have not independently verified citation or impact figures.
statement.conflict_note: No documented connection to Autor, Hanson, Katz or Dorn (B038), to Melitz or Helpman (B044), or to Kiyotaki or Moore (B037) appears in my profile. Disclosed connections are as follows. Peter Klenow, a long-running co-author, is a credited name on B047, which is neither my preferred part nor an alternative. Per Krusell (secretary) and John Hassler (chair) are IIES colleagues and frequent co-authors. I also collaborate with Philippe Aghion, who is not on the shortlist. My research on growth, structural change and firm dynamics is adjacent to B044 and B047, and I treat that as a reason for caution and not as evidence of merit. I do not think any disclosed tie requires me to limit participation on a particular ballot, and I note the chair's question about this. Conflicts are disclosed and not adjudicated.
